framework.name: Pólya's 4-Step Method
framework.one_liner: Understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back: four phases that force the unknown, the data and the condition into the open before anyone calculates.

slots.label: Phase
slots.description: Understand, Plan, Carry out, Look back. Polya's four phases, drawn as scaffolding rather than content.

slots.label: Problem
slots.description: The problem as posed, in the words in which it arrives.

slots.label: Unknown
slots.description: What is sought: the one quantity or object the whole exercise is for.

slots.label: Data
slots.description: What is given: the numbers, objects and notation the solver may use.

slots.label: Condition
slots.description: How the unknown and the data are connected; the relation the solution must respect.

slots.label: Plan
slots.description: The approach chosen, including the analogous or simpler problem it borrows from (Polya's 'related problem', marked attrs.kind = analogy).

slots.label: Step
slots.description: A verifiable step in carrying out the plan.

slots.label: Check
slots.description: How a step or the result is verified; in Polya's words, can you check the result, can you check the argument.

slots.label: Generalization
slots.description: Look back: the heuristic or result that transfers to other problems.

relations.label: in phase
relations.description: node belongs to one of the four phases

relations.label: states
relations.description: the problem as posed states the unknown, the data or the condition

relations.label: borrows from
relations.description: plan borrows from an analogous or simpler solved problem (a plan node with attrs.kind = analogy)

relations.label: uses
relations.description: a step or plan consumes a datum, a quantity from the problem, or the output of an earlier step

relations.label: verifies
relations.description: check verifies a step or the result

relations.label: generalizes
relations.description: generalization generalizes the plan or the result

examples.title: The diagonal of a rectangular parallelepiped
examples.summary: Polya's own worked example: the teacher's questions extract the unknown, the data and the condition, the student names the related problem but cannot use it, and the rest is supplied by the solver.

source.title: A classroom dialogue after Polya's worked example
source.text: Find the diagonal of a rectangular parallelepiped whose length, width and height are known. The teacher asks what the unknown is. The student answers: the length of the diagonal of a parallelepiped. What are the data? The length, the width and the height of the parallelepiped. What is the condition? The diagonal is the segment joining two opposite corners, so its length must be determined by the three edges and nothing else. The student draws a box, marks the three edges a, b and c, and draws the diagonal from one corner to the corner furthest from it. Asked whether he knows a related problem, he answers that the diagonal of a rectangle is found from its two sides. Asked whether that helps here, he says he does not yet see how a plane figure helps with a solid. He guesses that the answer is a plus b plus c, and sees at once that this cannot be right, because the diagonal of a square of side one would then be two.
source.attribution: After George Pólya, How to Solve It (1945), Part I; the dialogue is written for this example so that the fact nodes have something verbatim to quote.

nodes.label: Understand the problem
nodes.text: Phase 1. What is the unknown, what are the data, what is the condition. Polya's rule: you cannot answer a question you do not understand.

nodes.label: Devise a plan
nodes.text: Phase 2. Find the connection between the data and the unknown, usually by way of a related problem already solved, or an auxiliary element.

nodes.label: Carry out the plan
nodes.text: Phase 3. Execute the steps and check each one as you go. Can you see clearly that the step is correct.

nodes.label: Look back
nodes.text: Phase 4. Examine the solution obtained: check the result, check the argument, and ask whether the method can be used for another problem.

nodes.label: Diagonal of a parallelepiped
nodes.text: Find the diagonal of a rectangular parallelepiped whose length, width and height are known.
nodes.source_quote: Find the diagonal of a rectangular parallelepiped whose length, width and height are known.

nodes.label: Unknown: the diagonal's length
nodes.text: The unknown, named in answer to the teacher's first question: the length of the diagonal of a parallelepiped.
nodes.source_quote: the length of the diagonal of a parallelepiped

nodes.label: Given: length, width, height
nodes.text: The data: the length, the width and the height of the parallelepiped. Three numbers, and nothing else is given.
nodes.source_quote: The length, the width and the height of the parallelepiped

nodes.label: Figure drawn, edges a, b, c
nodes.text: The figure and the notation, which Polya counts as part of understanding the problem: a box is drawn, its three edges are marked a, b and c, and the diagonal is drawn from one corner to the corner furthest from it.
nodes.source_quote: The student draws a box, marks the three edges a, b and c

nodes.label: Three edges fix the diagonal
nodes.text: The condition: the diagonal is the segment joining two opposite corners, so its length must be determined by the three edges and nothing else.
nodes.source_quote: its length must be determined by the three edges and nothing else

nodes.label: Related: diagonal of a rectangle
nodes.text: The related problem the student produces when asked: the diagonal of a rectangle is found from its two sides. It has the same kind of unknown, one dimension lower.
nodes.source_quote: the diagonal of a rectangle is found from its two sides

nodes.label: Pythagoras twice, face diagonal
nodes.text: Introduce an auxiliary element, the diagonal of the base rectangle. It splits the solid problem into two plane problems, each of them the related problem: Pythagoras in the base, then Pythagoras in the vertical right triangle standing on it.
nodes.rationale: The source states the related problem and states that the student cannot use it: he 'does not yet see how a plane figure helps with a solid' (sentence 10). The bridge between them - draw the base diagonal and the solid becomes two right triangles - is exactly what the dialogue withholds, and it is close to forced once the figure, the notation and the related problem are all on the table.

nodes.label: First guess: a + b + c
nodes.text: A step taken before any plan exists: the student guesses that the answer is a plus b plus c.
nodes.source_quote: He guesses that the answer is a plus b plus c

nodes.label: Unit square refutes the guess
nodes.text: The check that kills the guess on the spot: for a square of side one the guess would make the diagonal two.
nodes.source_quote: the diagonal of a square of side one would then be two

nodes.label: Face diagonal e, e² = a² + b²
nodes.text: In the base rectangle the diagonal e satisfies e squared = a squared + b squared, by the Pythagorean theorem applied at the right angle between the edges a and b.
nodes.rationale: Forced by the plan together with the notation already in the source: the base is a rectangle of sides a and b, so its diagonal is fixed by the related problem the student himself named. The source never performs the step.

nodes.label: Right triangle on the base: e, c
nodes.text: The edge c is perpendicular to the base, so e and c are the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the diagonal d that was sought.
nodes.rationale: Follows from what a rectangular parallelepiped is, which the problem statement names but never unpacks. The perpendicularity is the permission to apply the related problem a second time, and it is the step that makes the plan work rather than merely sound plausible.

nodes.label: d = √(a² + b² + c²)
nodes.text: Therefore d squared = e squared + c squared = a squared + b squared + c squared, and the diagonal is the square root of the sum of the squares of the three edges.
nodes.rationale: Substitution of the two previous steps, arithmetic once they are granted. It is the answer to the unknown the source poses and never reaches.

nodes.label: Dimensions: degree one in length
nodes.text: Check the result by dimension: the expression is homogeneous of degree one in length, so the diagonal comes out in the units of the edges, and scaling every edge by k scales d by k.
nodes.rationale: Polya's 'can you check the result' applied to the formula the steps produce. The dialogue checks only the rejected guess, so every test of the answer itself is the reader's inference, not the source's.

nodes.label: Special cases: c = 0, a = b = c
nodes.text: Check the result against answers already known: with c = 0 the formula collapses to the diagonal of a rectangle, which is the related problem; with a = b = c it gives a times the square root of three, the diagonal of a cube. The expression is also symmetric in a, b and c, as the box is.
nodes.rationale: Each case is an answer that is known independently and that the formula has to reproduce, and the c = 0 case closes the loop back to the related problem stated in sentence 9. None of it happens in the dialogue.

nodes.label: Auxiliary element: 3-D to 2-D
nodes.text: The method rather than the formula is what transfers: when a problem in three dimensions resists, introduce an auxiliary element that reduces it to a problem in two dimensions you have already solved.
nodes.rationale: Generalises the plan that the steps executed. Polya's fourth phase asks whether the method can be used for another problem; the dialogue ends before that question is put.

nodes.label: Same argument in n dimensions
nodes.text: The same two-step argument runs in any number of dimensions: the diagonal of an n-dimensional box is the square root of the sum of the squares of its edges, by induction on the same auxiliary element.
nodes.rationale: The steps never used the fact that there are exactly three edges, only that one edge is perpendicular to the plane of the others, so the argument iterates. The source does not mention the extension.

edges.source_quote: The teacher asks what the unknown is. The student answers: the length of the diagonal of a parallelepiped.
What are the data? The length, the width and the height of the parallelepiped.
What is the condition? The diagonal is the segment joining two opposite corners, so its length must be determined by the three edges
its length must be determined by the three edges and nothing else
The diagonal is the segment joining two opposite corners, so its length must be determined by the three edges

edges.label: refutes
edges.source_quote: He guesses that the answer is a plus b plus c, and sees at once that this cannot be right, because the diagonal of a square of side one would then be two.

edges.rationale: The three edges marked a, b and c in sentence 8 are the three lengths given in sentence 5; the text names them in different words in adjacent sentences and never says they are the same three.
The guess a plus b plus c consumes exactly the three given lengths. The source states the guess but not that it is built out of the data.

edges.label: same unknown, 2-D
edges.rationale: The plan is the related problem applied twice. Sentence 10 says explicitly that the student cannot see the link, so the link is the inference.
First half of the plan: Pythagoras in the base rectangle.
The plan's auxiliary element is what makes this right triangle available.
Second half of the plan: Pythagoras in the vertical triangle, then substitution.
The step is written in the notation introduced with the figure in sentence 8.
The step uses the third marked edge c and the box drawn in sentence 8.
The leg of this triangle is the face diagonal computed in the previous step.
Substitutes the two legs of the triangle established in the previous step.
A dimensional test of the expression the step produced.
Special cases test the same expression against answers known in advance.
The c = 0 case is the related problem; the check consumes it as a known answer.
Names what the plan did in a form that does not mention boxes.
Extends the result, not the method, to n dimensions.
The expression is an answer only because the unknown was named as a length.
The dimensional check works because the data are three lengths.
The general heuristic is read off the one related problem the source supplies.
The extension replaces the three given lengths by n of them.

examples.title: What is six gigawatts of AMD chips worth?
examples.summary: A host poses a bounded sizing problem on air, two estimates four times apart are produced before anyone has a method, the method is then stated in full and never executed, and nobody looks back.

source.episode_title: OpenAI AMD deal, DevDay reactions, xAI's Memphis datacenter (Doug O'Laughlin, Celine Halioua)

examples.why_this_episode: A host states the unknown out loud ('can you estimate the dollar value of that'), the givens are quoted from the filing and from an analyst, and the plan is verbalised in order - watts per chip, divide into six gigawatts, multiply by price. Two incompatible estimates are produced before the plan exists, one is rejected without a reason, the plan is never carried out and nothing is looked back at, so the four phases are visible precisely by which of them the conversation skipped.

annotations.text: The plan's three steps, never taken

nodes.label: Understand the problem
nodes.text: Phase 1. What is the unknown, what are the data, what is the condition. Polya's rule: you cannot answer a question you do not understand.

nodes.label: Devise a plan
nodes.text: Phase 2. Find the connection between the data and the unknown, usually by way of a related problem already solved, or an auxiliary element.

nodes.label: Carry out the plan
nodes.text: Phase 3. Execute the steps and check each one as you go. Can you see clearly that the step is correct.

nodes.label: Look back
nodes.text: Phase 4. Examine the solution obtained: check the result, check the argument, and ask whether the method can be used for another problem.

nodes.label: 6 GW of AMD chips committed
nodes.text: The problem as posed, in units of power: under the terms of the deal OpenAI committed to purchasing six gigawatts worth of AMD chips.
nodes.source_quote: Under the terms of the deal, OpenAI committed to purchasing six gigawatts worth of AMD chips.

nodes.label: Unknown: dollar value of 6 GW
nodes.text: The unknown, put by a host to the show's researcher: what is six gigawatts of AMD chips worth in dollars, if the chips are MI-450 equivalents?
nodes.source_quote: six gigawatts of AMD chips. Can you estimate the dollar value of that if it's MI 40, 450 equivalence?

nodes.label: Orders denominated in energy
nodes.text: The condition, noticed in passing: GPU orders are now quoted in energy demand, so any dollar figure has to be reached through a conversion from power to chips.
nodes.source_quote: we're now just referring to GPU orders based on their energy demands

nodes.label: Tens of billions per gigawatt
nodes.text: A given from AMD itself: the plan costs tens of billions of dollars per gigawatt of computing capacity. The two companies did not disclose the overall expected cost.
nodes.source_quote: AMD said it costs tens of billions of dollars per gigawatt of computing capacity

nodes.label: $50B per gigawatt, recalled
nodes.text: A second per-gigawatt price, recalled by the researcher from an analyst: around fifty billion dollars per gigawatt. The attribution is unintelligible in the transcript and the number is never sourced on air.
nodes.source_quote: he said it's like around 50 billion per gigawatt

nodes.label: 1 GW MI-450 starts H2 next year
nodes.text: The ramp: OpenAI will begin with one gigawatt worth of MI-450 chips in the second half of next year, so the six gigawatts arrives in stages.
nodes.source_quote: open AI is going to begin with one gigawatt worth of MI 450 chips starting in the second half of next year to run its AI models.

nodes.label: AMD: tens of billions by 2027
nodes.text: A given from the other side of the deal: Lisa Su told investors the agreement would give AMD tens of billions of dollars of revenue by 2027.
nodes.source_quote: would give AMD tens of billions of dollars of revenue by 2027
nodes.source_ref: host reading the WSJ on Lisa Su's investor call, L1676-L1678

nodes.label: Plan: watts per chip, then price
nodes.text: The plan, stated out loud and in order: find the energy use of a single MI-450, divide six gigawatts by it to get the number of chips, then multiply by the price of a chip.
nodes.source_quote: what is the energy use of a single MI-450, and then divide that by six gigawatts to get me, like, how many chips are they going to buy, and then what's the price of the chip, so multiply that

nodes.label: Related: 1 GW ≈ 800,000 homes
nodes.text: The same episode performs the conversion for electricity rather than for silicon: a new plant capable of generating over a gigawatt, enough to power around 800,000 homes.
nodes.source_quote: capable of generating over a gigawatt of electricity enough to power around 800,000 homes
nodes.source_ref: host reading the WSJ on xAI in Memphis, L1744

nodes.label: Estimate 1: almost $100B
nodes.text: The first estimate, produced from AMD's per-gigawatt figure before anyone had asked what the answer depended on: almost a hundred billion dollars.
nodes.source_quote: So we're looking at almost a hundred billion dollar deal

nodes.label: Estimate 2: $400B?
nodes.text: The second estimate, produced from the recalled fifty billion per gigawatt: a four hundred billion dollar deal.
nodes.source_quote: Wait, so this is like a 400 billion dollar deal?

nodes.label: “That's totally wrong”
nodes.text: The host rejects his own second estimate at once, without saying what is wrong with it or what would replace it.
nodes.source_quote: I think, wait, that's totally wrong

nodes.label: Step not taken: watts per chip
nodes.text: Establish the power draw of one MI-450 as deployed, measured at the rack so that cooling and networking are inside the number. This is the first input the stated plan asks for.
nodes.rationale: The plan at L1698-L1712 names this as its first input and nobody supplies it; the semiconductor analyst in the next segment is asked about where the power will come from instead (L2286). Measuring at the rack rather than at the die is forced by the data: six gigawatts is facility power, so the divisor has to be facility power per accelerator.

nodes.label: Step not taken: chip count
nodes.text: Divide six gigawatts of committed capacity by the per-accelerator draw to get the number of MI-450s the order covers.
nodes.rationale: Second step of the stated plan, never carried out in the episode. The quoted plan inverts its own division ('divide that by six gigawatts'), which is another reason the step has to be reconstructed rather than read off.

nodes.label: Step not taken: count × price
nodes.text: Multiply the accelerator count by the price of one MI-450 to get the dollar value of the six-gigawatt commitment, which is the unknown as posed.
nodes.rationale: Third step of the stated plan and the one that would answer the question at L1690-L1692. Derived because the multiplication is never performed and no unit price is ever stated by anyone on the show.

nodes.label: Two estimates differ fourfold
nodes.text: The two figures already on the table are incompatible: about a hundred billion read off 'tens of billions per gigawatt', and four hundred billion asserted from fifty billion per gigawatt, which would in any case give three hundred billion across six gigawatts. At most one of them survives.
nodes.rationale: Both estimates are facts in the source. That they exclude each other, and that fifty billion times six gigawatts is three hundred billion rather than four hundred, is arithmetic the episode never performs. This is Polya's 'examine the result' applied to two results at once.

nodes.label: Check against AMD's guidance
nodes.text: Bound the per-gigawatt price with AMD's own disclosure. Tens of billions of dollars of revenue by 2027 cannot sit under a six-gigawatt order priced at fifty billion per gigawatt unless most of the capacity lands after 2027, is bought through cloud partners, or is priced far below the recalled figure.
nodes.rationale: Uses the revenue guidance at L1676-L1678 and the phased start at L1600-L1602 as an independent bound on the per-gigawatt number at L1694. The source states all three and never puts them side by side.

nodes.label: Convert the unit before pricing
nodes.text: The heuristic that transfers: when an order is denominated in a unit you cannot price - gigawatts, tokens, square feet of fab - do not estimate in that unit. Convert it into countable physical things first, price the things, and treat the conversion rate itself as the thing being estimated.
nodes.rationale: Generalises the plan the host states and never executes (L1698-L1712) together with the conversion the same episode performs for electricity but not for silicon (L1744). Polya's fourth phase; the episode never reaches it, so all of it is inference.
nodes.idea: AI infrastructure is announced in gigawatts but underwritten in accelerators and dollars, so a per-gigawatt bill of materials - watts, racks, accelerators and price per accelerator generation - is a product that analysts, lenders and reporters on this beat currently rebuild by hand for every announcement.

nodes.label: The fourfold spread is the gap
nodes.text: The size of the disagreement is itself the finding. A live fourfold spread on the headline value of an agreement both parties call definitive says the conversion layer between energy, silicon and dollars is missing rather than merely unpublished.
nodes.rationale: Reads the contradiction found in tk1 as a market fact rather than a slip. Contestable, since the spread could be ordinary day-one noise; the evidence for the stronger reading is that nobody closes it on air with a semiconductor analyst waiting in the next segment.
nodes.idea: The spread itself is the product: a live, dated measure of how far apart the credible readings of an announced deal sit - a hundred billion against four hundred - is a signal an underwriter, a lender or a trader would pay for on its own, before any single number is settled.

edges.rationale: The host's remark at L1400-L1402 says orders are quoted in energy; that this is what stands between the question and an answer in dollars is the framework's reading, not a claim anyone makes.
The per-gigawatt price is usable only because the order is denominated in power. The source puts the two facts three hundred lines apart and never joins them.

edges.label: same conversion
edges.rationale: Converting a gigawatt into 800,000 homes is the already-solved version of the conversion the plan needs. The link crosses two segments of the episode and two speakers' material, and nobody on air draws it.
First input named by the plan.
The division named by the plan.
The multiplication named by the plan, which would answer the unknown.
The divisor is the output of the previous step.
The multiplicand is the chip count from the previous step.
The hundred-billion estimate is one of the two results being compared.
The four-hundred-billion estimate is the other, and it fails its own arithmetic.
AMD's revenue guidance is an independent bound on the price that produced this estimate.
The check consumes the revenue guidance as its bound; the source never uses it as one.
The phased start is what lets some of the six gigawatts fall outside the guidance window, so the check needs it.
States what the plan was an instance of, in a form that does not mention gigawatts.
Turns the contradiction the check found into a claim about the market rather than about the speakers.
The step is a step only because the unknown was posed in dollars.
The transferable heuristic is read off the one conversion the episode actually performs.
The spread is measured from the two estimates the speakers produced.
